basis:
The executable change is identical in both submissions — same single-instruction fix (`jr z,ttNoCut` -> `jr c,ttNoCut`) at the same site, plus the same stale-header correction ("8 KB / 1024 buckets at 0x6000" -> "4 KB / 512 buckets at TT_BASE (0xC000)"). Neither touches a spec file, a test, or any other module, so there is no direct process artefact (no proof, no conformance-suite delta) to key on. The only discriminating material is comment prose, which makes any inference weak.

Two small tells lean me toward X:

1. X does not merely correct the stale layout comment, it *reconciles the documented claim against the code constants that establish it* and records the divergence: "see ttAddr, which masks the key to 0x1FF, and ttClear, which zeroes 0x1000 bytes. (This line used to read "8 KB / 1024 buckets at 0x6000"; it never matched the code.)" Naming the two concrete implementation facts (mask 0x1FF => 512 buckets; clear length 0x1000 => 4 KB) that jointly pin the layout, and explicitly flagging that the written spec never matched the implementation, reads like someone whose process requires a maintained description to agree with the code and who logs the mismatch when it is repaired. Y makes the same correction as a bare edit, with no justification and no note that the old text was wrong.

2. X states the fixed predicate as a biconditional — "cp (hl) computes entDepth - curDepth, so CF=1 <=> the entry is shallower than what we are searching now" — i.e. flag semantics as an iff, which is the shape of a proof obligation. Y states the same fact as a one-directional implication ("CF=1 means ttEntDepth < ttCurDepth").

Counter-evidence I weighed against this: Y uses the exact source identifiers (ttEntDepth/ttCurDepth) where X abbreviates, which is arguably the more code-literal habit; and both comments include the same counterfactual fault analysis of the wrong predicate (JR Z admits shallower entries and pins the search at the previous iterative-deepening depth), so neither has a monopoly on mechanism-level reasoning. X's phrasing "the strength setting would do nothing" also echoes the bug-report title, which is as consistent with test-driven work as with spec work.

Given that the repair itself is indistinguishable and the signal is entirely stylistic, "cannot tell" is a defensible answer here; I name X only because of the spec-vs-code reconciliation, and I would not defend it strongly.
